opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important things, actually. When people only read about AI, or hear about it secondhand, it's very abstract. You hear "AI is going to be powerful," and it's just words. It doesn't really land. But when you interact with it yourself, when you see what it can do and also where it falls short, your intuition changes. You develop a feel for it.

And I think that matters a great deal, because the arrival of very powerful AI is going to affect everyone. It's not something that should be decided by a small number of people in a few labs without the rest of the world having any felt sense of what's happening. If people can see the technology improving, year after year, they can form their own views. Governments can respond. Institutions can adapt. There's time to adjust, rather than everything arriving all at once as a shock.

There's also a very practical side. When you deploy, you learn things you simply cannot learn in the lab. You see how people actually use the system, what goes wrong, what kinds of misuse appear, what people find genuinely helpful. That feedback is incredibly valuable for making the systems safer and better.

So it's both: it helps society understand what's coming and prepare for it, and it helps us, the people building it, understand what we've actually built. I think a gradual, incremental exposure is much better than keeping everything hidden and then one day releasing something extremely powerful into a world that has no intuition for it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that reading or hearing about AI is abstract and “doesn't really land,” while interacting with it and seeing what it can do changes your intuition.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they're related.

The first is that it's very hard to reason about AI in the abstract. If you just tell people, "this technology is going to be very powerful, it's going to change a lot of things," it's an abstract statement. People nod, and then they go on with their lives. But when you actually sit down and talk to the model, and it does something that you didn't expect it could do, that experience is different. It changes something in your understanding in a way that no amount of argument can. So in some sense, the public experiencing AI directly is the only way for society as a whole to really understand what's coming, rather than just a small group of researchers.

The second reason is that I think it's important that the adjustment happens gradually. If you imagine a world where AI is developed in secret, and it becomes very capable, and then one day it's released and it's already extremely powerful, that would be a very large shock. Whereas if people can see it getting better step by step, year by year, then institutions, governments, businesses, individuals, everyone has a chance to think about it, to argue about it, to form opinions, to adapt. I think that's healthier. The disagreements that people have now, about what these systems can and cannot do, about what they should be allowed to do, those disagreements are valuable. It's better to have them while the stakes are still lower.

And the third reason, which is more of a research reason, is that you learn things from contact with reality. When many people use these systems, you discover failure modes that you never would have anticipated in a lab. You discover that the model is being used in ways you didn't imagine. Some of those uses are good and some of them are concerning, and both kinds are informative. So there's a sense in which the public experience of AI is part of the process of making it safer and better, not just a consequence of it.

Now, I'll say that this isn't unconditional. There is a question of how capable a system has to be before the calculus changes, before the risks of wide access start to outweigh the benefits of the gradual adaptation I was describing. I don't think we're at that point, but I think it's a real question and it's worth taking seriously. But for the systems we have today, I think the benefits are quite clear.

r001.rationale: It contrasts abstractly telling people about AI with having them interact with a model and see an unexpected capability, saying that direct experience changes their understanding in a way argument cannot.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful for people to experience the technology firsthand, because it’s difficult to understand something this new from a description. You can hear that an AI is capable, but when you interact with it, you start to develop an intuition for what that means—where it’s useful, where it makes mistakes, and how it might affect your life.

And the public needs to be part of the conversation about what happens next. Direct experience gives people a more concrete basis for that conversation. It also gives us feedback: people will find uses and problems that we wouldn’t have anticipated.

r001.rationale: The response says firsthand interaction builds intuition that descriptions cannot provide, but it does not state that seeing AI demonstrate its capabilities is far more compelling than reading about them.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it’s very hard to understand a technology like this in the abstract. You can hear that AI is going to be important, but when you actually use it, you start to develop an intuition for what it can do, where it fails, and how it might affect your life.

And I think that matters because the public should have a voice in what happens with AI. Direct experience gives people a better basis for that conversation. It also gives us a chance to learn from how people use these systems, while the systems are still relatively limited.

r001.rationale: The response says direct use builds intuition and is easier to understand than AI in the abstract, but it does not state that demonstrations are far more compelling than reading descriptions.
